newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Abkhazia vows to hold poll despite U.N. warnings.
newsitem.headline: Abkhazia vows to hold poll despite U.N. warnings.

text.p: The leader of Georgia's Black Sea province of Abkhazia said on Tuesday he was determined to press on with elections planned next month, despite fears the poll could spark renewed violence in the breakaway region.

Per Kallstrom, the chief military observer for the 133-member U.N. mission in Abkhazia, said the vote could trigger new confrontation in the region, where some 10,000 people have died in ethnic violence since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Self-styled Abkhaz president Vladislav Ardzindba dismissed such warnings. "There will be an election. Nothing will happen. There are a lot of idiots in the U.N.," he told Reuters.
Kallstrom said the United Nations had denounced the planned poll because refugees, who made up nearly half Abkhazia's pre-war population, had fled separatist violence and were unable to participate.

"If the vote is held, there is the risk of an escalation. There will be a lot of violence from the Georgian side and the Abkhaz will retaliate. If worse comes to worst, we could be witnessing a new war in the months to come," he said.

"The thing is that the only ones who can vote are those who are here now. Most of the population is outside Abkhazia. The election is contrary to the aims of the outside world, which demands the prompt return of the refugees."
Abkhazia, a lush subtropical region on Georgia's northwestern border, has run itself as an independent state since 1993 and Ardzindba has set elections for November 23.
His administration, backed by covert Russian military help and volunteers among ethnic kin in Russia's north Caucasus region, ousted poorly disciplined Georgian government troops in 1993.
Since then occasional violence has punctuated an uneasy three-year calm enforced by 2,500 Russian peacekeepers along a de facto confrontation line.

Negotiations have so far failed to produce a peace plan because the Abkhaz, who say they were forced into Georgia's Soviet-era borders by dictator Josef Stalin, have not been able to agree with Tbilisi on the region's political status.
The central electoral commission said 78 candidates, 60 of whom are ethnic Abkhaz, would contest 35 single-mandate constituencies in November..
It put the electorate at about 200,000 people, comprising some 100,000 Abkhaz, an ancient north Caucasus ethnic group and many ethnic Russians and Armenians.
